title: Puzzle day
goal: I can choose a way to start a puzzle. I can read picture graphs and logic grids. I can check my answer against every clue.

learn.intro: A puzzle is easier when you know how to start. Draw it. List it in order. Make a table. Then check every clue.

example.problem: Lily has 7 coins. Each coin is 10¢ or 20¢. They are worth $1.10 altogether. How many of each coin?
steps: Start with 7 coins of 10¢. That is 70¢.
Swap one 10¢ for a 20¢. The total goes up by 10¢ each time.
Stop when the total is 110¢: 3 coins of 10¢ and 4 coins of 20¢.

howto.title: Ways to start
steps: Draw it: a picture or a bar.
List it: write every case in order.

facts.title: Tips
lines: Logic grid: tick one box. Cross out the rest of its row and column.
List in order so no case is missed.

try.text: The key of a graph says each picture is 5 children. Maths has 6 pictures. How many chose maths? {b}
try.explanation: Each picture is 5 children. 6 pictures: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. So 30 children chose maths.

items.text: Read the picture graph. Look at the key first.

parts.label: b
parts.text: More children chose football than swimming: {b}

items.explanation: Each picture stands for 5 children. (a) Chess has 3 pictures: 3 × 5 = 15. (b) Football has 2 more pictures than swimming: 2 × 5 = 10 more. (c) 6 + 4 + 3 + 5 = 18 pictures, and 18 × 5 = 90 children.

items.text: 75 children chose a club. The Art row is not drawn yet.
items.explanation: 75 children is 75 ÷ 5 = 15 pictures altogether. The other rows have 5 + 3 + 4 = 12 pictures. So Art needs 15 - 12 = 3 pictures, which is 15 children.

items.text: I am a number between 40 and 60. I am in the 5 times table. My digits add up to 10. What number am I? {b}
items.explanation: Numbers between 40 and 60 in the 5 times table: 45, 50, 55. Digit sums: 4 + 5 = 9, 5 + 0 = 5, 5 + 5 = 10. So the number is 55.

items.text: Ali counts the pets in his street. He makes a tally chart. A group of 5 has 4 strokes and a slash.
items.explanation: Count in 5s for each group with a slash, then add the strokes. Dogs: 5 + 5 + 2 = 12. Cats: 5 + 2 = 7. Fish: 4. (b) 12 - 7 = 5. (c) 7 + 12 + 4 = 23.

items.text: The cards 7, 0 and 5 can build 3-digit numbers. Use each card once.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The greatest is {b} and the smallest is {b}.

items.explanation: 0 cannot be first. Start with 5: 507, 570. Start with 7: 705, 750. (b) Greatest 750, smallest 507. (c) 705 and 750 are between 600 and 800: 2 numbers.

items.text: Ben has 6 coins. Each coin is 10¢ or 20¢. They are worth $1.10 altogether. Fill in the table.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ben has {b} coin of 10¢ and {b} coins of 20¢.

items.explanation: Each swap of a 10¢ for a 20¢ adds 10¢: 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 110. $1.10 is the last column: 1 coin of 10¢ and 5 coins of 20¢. Check: 10 + 100 = 110 and 1 + 5 = 6 coins.

items.text: Ali, Mei and Ravi each have 1 fruit: an apple, a banana or a mango. Mei has the mango. Ali does not have the apple.
items.explanation: Mei has the mango, so cross out mango for Ali and Ravi. Ali does not have the apple and not the mango, so Ali has the banana. Ravi has the apple.

items.text: Mei cuts a pizza into 6 equal slices. She eats 1/6 and Ali eats 2/6. Each slice is 100 g.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The mass of the pizza left is {b} g.

items.text: Aisha buys 3 pens. Each pen costs $1.20. She pays with a $5 note.
A hall has 4 rows of 10 chairs. 28 children sit down.
items.explanation: (a) 4 rows of 10: 4 × 10 = 40. (b) 40 - 28 = 12 empty chairs.

items.text: Ali, Mei, Siti and Ben like swimming, chess, art or tennis, one each. Mei likes chess. Ali does not like chess or art. Siti does not like swimming or tennis. Ben does not like tennis.
items.explanation: Mei likes chess. Siti does not like swimming or tennis, and chess is taken, so Siti likes art. Ali does not like chess or art, so Ali likes swimming or tennis. Ben does not like tennis, and chess and art are taken, so Ben likes swimming. Then Ali likes tennis.
items.hint: Tick Mei and chess. Cross out the rest of its row and column.

items.text: The key was lost. Apples have 7 pictures and pears have 3. 20 more children chose apples.
items.explanation: Apples have 7 - 3 = 4 more pictures than pears. 4 pictures are 20 children, so 1 picture is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 children. Apples: 7 × 5 = 35. Pears: 3 × 5 = 15. Check: 35 - 15 = 20.
items.hint: 4 more pictures is 20 children. How many in 1 picture?

items.text: Mei saves $2 on day 1, $4 on day 2, $6 on day 3, and so on. Ali saves $5 every day. Compare the totals saved so far.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mei first has more than Ali on day {b}.

items.explanation: Mei saves 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 so her totals are 2, 6, 12, 20, 30. Ali saves 5 a day: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. On day 4 they are level at $20. On day 5 Mei has $30 and Ali has $25, so Mei has $5 more.
items.hint: Add each day to the total of the day before.

items.text: Beyond: half a picture. Each picture stands for 10 children, so half a picture stands for 5 children.
items.explanation: (a) 3 pictures are 30 and half a picture is 5: 35. (b) 2 pictures are 20 and half a picture is 5: 25. (c) 35 - 25 = 10.
items.hint: 3 pictures is 30. Add the half picture.

items.text: Ali has one 5¢ coin, one 10¢ coin and two 20¢ coins. He pays with one or more of them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many different amounts can he pay? {b}

items.explanation: All 4 coins are worth 5 + 10 + 20 + 20 = 55¢, so 60¢ is too much. The amounts are 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50 and 55: 11 amounts. Every multiple of 5 from 5¢ to 55¢ works.

items.text: Make your own logic puzzle. Three children have a cat, a dog and a fish. Write 2 clues so only ONE answer fits. Many answers are right.

answer.text: Open. Example: Ali, Mei and Ravi have a cat, a dog and a fish. Mei has the fish. Ali does not have the cat. Then Ali has the dog and Ravi has the cat.

items.explanation: A good puzzle has exactly one answer. Example: Mei has the fish (so Ali and Ravi have the cat and the dog). Ali does not have the cat, so Ali has the dog and Ravi has the cat. Try to find a second answer: there is none.
items.hint: Pick the answer first. Then write clues that rule out the rest.

items.text: Ali buys 8 stickers. Small stickers cost 30¢. Large stickers cost 50¢. He pays $3.40 altogether.

parts.label: a
parts.text: He buys {b} small stickers and {b} large stickers.

items.explanation: 8 small stickers cost 8 × 30¢ = $2.40. Each swap of a small for a large adds 20¢: $2.60, $2.80, $3.00, $3.20, $3.40. That is 5 swaps, so 5 large and 3 small. Check: 90¢ + $2.50 = $3.40. The totals go up in 20¢ steps from $2.40, so $3.30 is never a total.
items.hint: Start with 8 small stickers. Each swap adds 20¢.

items.text: Each picture stands for 10 children. How many children chose Tuesday? {b}
items.explanation: Tuesday has 5 pictures. Each picture is 10 children. 5 × 10 = 50 children.

items.text: Use the digit cards 1, 0 and 4 once each. How many 3-digit numbers can you make? {b}
items.explanation: 0 cannot be first. Start with 1: 104, 140. Start with 4: 401, 410. That is 4 numbers.

items.text: Ali, Ben and Mei have red, blue and green. Mei has blue. Ali does not have red. Ben has {b}
items.explanation: Mei has blue. Ali does not have red, so Ali has green. Ben has red.

items.text: A pizza has 12 slices. 5/12 is eaten. What fraction is left? {b}
